title: AI Could Do My First Job. Not My Last.
gist: Jason Furman argues AI could replace much of the analytic work of the 35-person Council of Economic Advisers (about ten humans plus AI), especially junior roles, while humans keep meeting- and coalition-driven jobs. He weighs Jevons-style demand effects, the threat to the junior training pipeline and his own mixed feelings about AI.

themes.theme: AI can replace most analytic staff work at CEA

insights.claim: Furman believes most of what the White House Council of Economic Advisers did under his 2013-2017 leadership could now be done by about ten people plus AI, versus a staff of about 35.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Signals large headcount compression in analytic knowledge-work organizations.

insights.claim: He told Neil Irwin he would choose today's AI systems over 20 staff with current and future Ph.D.s to run the CEA, and now thinks that figure may have understated the case.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: A prominent senior economist openly endorses AI over junior-to-mid economist headcount.

insights.claim: As a junior CEA staffer under Clinton, Furman judges AI guided by seniors like Stiglitz and Yellen could do 95 percent of what he did: short analyses, data tracking, memos, report drafting, forecast work and speechwriting.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Entry-level analytic tasks are the most automatable.

insights.claim: AI exposure depends on task mix, not seniority or intelligence: roles of meetings, briefings, testimony and coalition-building are safe, while computer-based analysis and writing roles are exposed, even for experienced senior economists.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Screen jobs by share of interpersonal/coordination work rather than title or pay.

insights.claim: Junior staff at the National Economic Council are probably safer from AI than even senior CEA staff because NEC work is running meetings, building coalitions and implementing policy.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Exposure measures by occupation or seniority can miss within-sector differences.

insights.claim: AI poses more threat to some of the smartest people in academia, such as mathematicians, than to people in many other disciplines, and some colleagues wonder if their days as active researchers are numbered.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: High-skill research jobs are not automatically insulated.

themes.theme: Current AI capability evidence (Furman's agent experiments)

insights.claim: Furman's Paperwright multi-agent engine turned the prompt 'data centers and electricity prices' into a 65-page economics paper in about six hours, with a mathematical model, county-level data analysis, references and a replication package.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Agentic pipelines now produce thesis-grade research for hours of compute and little human input.

insights.claim: He rates the paper not publishable even in a mid-level journal, but would expect a Summa-range grade as a Harvard senior thesis.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Calibrates quality: strong undergraduate-level, not frontier research.

insights.claim: His Blogwright experiment produces think-tank-style blogs he judges to be among the better versions of the genre, and he expects a simple chatbot prompt to beat his multi-step architecture within a year or two.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Scaffolding advantages erode fast, so value shifts to the base models.

insights.claim: Almost every Econvitals email is AI-written and sent without his review, and he finds them timely, reasonably comprehensive and generally accurate.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Unsupervised AI content production is already workable in economic commentary.

insights.claim: He prefers AI-generated blog posts to human-written ones for getting up to speed, because human pieces may be out of date or contain inaccurate numbers, and AI used properly can make fewer mistakes than people.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Information-product demand may shift toward AI-generated explainers.

insights.claim: Complaints about hallucinations and Wikipedia repackaging describe weaker models from a year or two ago and are barely relevant to agentic AI today.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Skeptics are anchoring on stale capabilities.

insights.claim: Furman still expects his own posts to be more interesting than AI output, and says the human-written pieces his Morning Note links to also beat anything AI writes.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Humans keep an edge in original, interesting writing for now.

insights.claim: Both over-reliance (slop nobody understands) and under-reliance (more mistakes, less ambition) are errors, and he sees more under-users among economists and think tankers.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Adoption gaps in professional services may still be large.

themes.theme: Elasticity of demand and Jevons paradox

insights.claim: Whether technology cuts or raises labor demand depends on the elasticity of demand for output: farming employment shrank as food demand stayed flat, while accounting hiring grew as business demand for accounting services soared, though that has fallen off lately.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Sector outcomes hinge on demand elasticity, so favor sectors with elastic demand for AI-cheapened output.

insights.claim: For CEA, demand elasticity is doubtful because its output was already free and its clients (NEC, Congress, media) could do much of the work themselves, so demand could fall rather than rise.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Captive or low-elasticity internal-service functions are most at risk of shrinking.

insights.claim: Humans have consistently underestimated demand for improved goods over time, since people can picture living standards twice as good but not ten or a hundred times as good, so Furman may be underestimating how many people AI-enabled analysis will need.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Bullish counterweight: unmet demand could absorb displaced labor.

insights.claim: Furman has talked to dozens of Harvard and other colleagues and found none who cites Jevons paradox in hiring research assistants; most think they need the same number, fewer or none, and he himself no longer has a full-time RA.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Anecdotal evidence of falling demand for junior research labor.

insights.claim: Hosseini Maasoum and Lichtinger found junior employment down about 9 percent at AI-adopting firms, while the Yale Budget Lab team under Martha Gimbel sees no occupational mix shift clearly lining up with AI.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Evidence on AI job displacement is still conflicting and early.

insights.claim: Furman would not be surprised if the optimal CEA were about half its current size, with more senior staff chosen for interpersonal skills and ability to manage AI agents, and expects the optimal number to be more likely to fall than rise.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Hiring will tilt toward senior, AI-managing generalists with fewer entry roles.

insights.claim: Statistical agencies are vastly underresourced, and Econvitals depends on the thousands of people who collect and analyze data there, so efficiency drives should not always mean cutting staff.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Data-producing public functions remain a human-resource bottleneck for the AI economy.

insights.claim: Furman says CEA's training role has had real though not purely causal impact, citing alumni who became Nobel and John Bates Clark winners, a Treasury Secretary and a CBO Director, much of which is selection.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Apprenticeship pipelines have value that is hard to measure.

insights.claim: The paper 'Pyramids, Diamonds, and Oscillations' by Guido Friebel and coauthors models AI making firms freeze junior hiring in the short run and possibly shifting permanently from a pyramid of many juniors to a diamond with a bulge of experienced mid-level people.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Org charts may reshape to diamonds, hurting entry-level labor markets first.

insights.claim: Taxpayer-funded jobs where the bulk of work could be done by AI cannot be justified just for training, and 'training' by botsitting is questionable; research grantors also seek maximum output rather than pipeline-building.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Public and grant funding unlikely to subsidize junior roles made redundant by AI.

insights.claim: Under Becker's model workers pay for general training through lower wages, which works if an associate produces $300,000 but earns $200,000, but breaks down if the associate produces about zero, since nobody would pay the firm $100,000 a year to be trained.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Economics of apprenticeship in finance and professional services is under threat, with training to be paid explicitly.

insights.claim: Furman expects the pipeline to need explicit funding through fellowships and training grants rather than relying on organizations to keep hiring people they no longer need, and says surplus government funds should go where skills are needed, such as public health, AI safety or national security.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Policy direction: explicit training subsidies instead of implicit make-work.

insights.claim: Furman, formerly an AI accelerationist who said the biggest worry was not having enough AI, would now be seriously tempted to press a button freezing AI for decades, though he would not actually press it.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Notable shift in tone among mainstream economists on AI.
insights.quote: "The biggest worry I have about AI is that we will not have enough of it."
insights.locator: I Don't Know the Right Ratio

insights.claim: He argues AI's downside falls mostly on the high-income or high-meaning knowledge workers, while poorer people, the sick and those hit by climate change have more upside than downside from innovation and productivity growth.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Global welfare framing favors continued AI progress despite concentrated losses in white-collar work.
insights.locator: I Don't Know the Right Ratio

insights.claim: His advice is to use AI better while focusing on uniquely human value added, such as management and interpersonal skills, and continuing to challenge oneself so skills are not offloaded to AI, though it may not suffice.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Skill premium shifts toward AI management and interpersonal coordination.
insights.locator: I Don't Know the Right Ratio

insights.claim: Furman defers his broader public policy response to AI labor disruption to a later post.
insights.speaker: Jason Furman
insights.so_what: Policy prescriptions are still to come.
insights.locator: I Don't Know the Right Ratio
